title: The Mill on the Floss: A Literary Discussion

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked — a close, passionate, occasionally argumentative look at one of the great novels of the nineteenth century.
George Eliot published The Mill on the Floss in 1860, and it has been unsettling readers — in the best possible way — ever since.
It is a novel about childhood, about belonging, about the crushing weight of family and provincial life — and about one of the most vivid protagonists in all of English fiction: Maggie Tulliver.
Joining me today are three readers who know this novel deeply and argue about it brilliantly.

Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than almost anyone alive — he hears prose the way a musician hears a score, and his instinct for when George Eliot is being funny is, frankly, irreplaceable.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every novel as an anatomy of power — who benefits, who suffers, and who the system was built to protect.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has been arguing with it ever since — she cares about what it feels like to sit with these pages, sentence by sentence.
We begin where the novel begins to show us who Maggie truly is — in childhood, in flight, in imagination.
Oliver, this passage — Maggie resolving to run away to the gypsies after Tom rejects her — what does it do for you as a performer?
It is one of the great comic set-ups in Victorian fiction — and George Eliot knows exactly what she is doing.
The narrator gives us this magnificent opening sentence: Maggie's intentions, as usual, were on a larger scale than Tom imagined.
"Maggie's intentions, as usual, were on a larger scale than Tom imagined."
That "as usual" is doing extraordinary work — it is a tiny aside that tells you everything about this child and everyone around her.
When I read aloud the passage where she resolves to send her father a letter via a small gypsy — who would "run away without telling where she was" — I can never quite keep a straight face.
It is comedy, yes — but it is also completely serious to Maggie in that moment, and that doubleness is where the genius lives.
What strikes me, rereading this, is how carefully Eliot has constructed Maggie's logic — it is not random childish fancy.
Maggie has been told she is "like a gypsy" and "half wild" — so she takes those words and turns them into a destination.
The narrator tells us the passage about her mind so precisely — I keep returning to it.
"In travelling over her small mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge."
That phrase — "her small mind" — is heartbreaking and funny at the same time.
Eliot is both indulgent and clear-eyed about this child — she loves Maggie and sees her completely.
I want to hold onto something Caroline said — about the words used to describe Maggie: gypsy, half wild.
These are not neutral descriptors — they are the language a provincial bourgeois community uses to mark a child as not quite fitting, not quite manageable.
What's devastating is that Maggie internalises it — she doesn't resist the label, she runs toward it.
And then look at what happens when she actually reaches the gypsies — the fantasy collapses into something closer to gothic horror.
The narrator tells us that she had begun to think — and this is extraordinary —
"she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking."
"Gradual cooking." George Eliot is writing comedy of absolute precision there — but the fear underneath it is real.
The place Maggie ran to for freedom turns out to be another place that terrifies her — which is, I'd argue, the novel's central mechanism in miniature.
"Gradual cooking" — I have read that line out loud to audiences and waited for the laugh, and it always comes, and then there's a little catch of unease immediately after.
What Daniel is pointing to is true — but I think Eliot is also doing something specifically theological in that passage.
The fierce-eyed old man becomes the Devil in Maggie's imagination — and then the narrator adds, with perfect deadpan irony, that she wondered
"whether, if the Devil were really present, he would know her thoughts."
That is a child's theology — but it is also a child's privacy, a child's desperate inner life asserting itself even in the face of mortal terror.
And all of this — the escape plan, the gradual cooking, the Devil — comes from a child who has read the dictionary for want of other books.
Eliot tells us that Maggie's thoughts were, and I love this phrase,
"the oddest mixture of clear-eyed acumen and blind dreams."
That is Maggie's portrait in nine words — and I would argue it stays true of her for the rest of the novel.
Clear-eyed acumen and blind dreams — that tension, I think, is going to haunt us all the way through this conversation.
We have established who Maggie is in childhood — this extraordinary mind in a world that cannot quite hold her.
In our next segment, we turn to the world that surrounds her — the Tullivers, the Dodsons, and the social machinery of St Ogg's.

segments.title: The Weight of Water: Maggie's Hunger for More

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm joined today by three wonderful readers of this novel — each bringing a completely different lens to the same extraordinary book.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than almost anyone alive, and he hears the prose the way a musician hears a score.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads fiction as a map of class and power — and he finds Eliot more radical than she is usually given credit for.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has been rereading this novel since her teens and brings to it both the devotion of a longtime reader and the precision of a close critic.
Our focus today is Maggie Tulliver's hunger — her hunger for knowledge, for love, for a world wider than the one she's been given.
And we're going to trace that hunger through some of the novel's most revealing childhood passages.
Caroline, let's begin with you — because you've always said the jealousy passages are where we first see the full complexity of Maggie.
Yes — and I think these passages are startling in a way readers sometimes underestimate.
Eliot doesn't flinch from showing Maggie's uglier impulses — the capacity for cruelty, not just the capacity for love.
There's a passage I keep coming back to, about little Lucy Deane.
"Maggie would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse."
That image — the little white mouse — is absolutely perfect.
It gives Lucy a kind of helpless prettiness, and it shows how Maggie had positioned herself as the generous one, the protector.
But when Tom prefers Lucy, that whole self-image collapses — and what comes up instead is the desire to pinch her.
It's funny and it's horrible and it's absolutely true to how children work.
And what Eliot understands — which a lesser novelist wouldn't — is that Maggie's fury isn't really about Lucy at all.
It's about Tom. It's always about Tom.
The line that gets me is the parenthetical logic she uses to justify herself.
"Tom had always been quite indifferent to Lucy before, and it had been left to Maggie to pet and make much of her."
There's a whole moral philosophy packed into that clause — she's not being cruel, she's been betrayed.
Eliot gives us Maggie's self-justification entirely straight-faced, and we are expected to find it both ridiculous and completely understandable.
That's the double-vision Eliot has on her characters that makes the novel so rich to read aloud.
I'd push on that a bit — because I think there's something structurally important happening in that scene, beyond the psychology.
Maggie is already learning the lesson she will spend the whole novel trying to resist — that Tom's approval is the currency she must earn.
And Lucy is the mirror in which that lesson is reflected — the pretty, compliant girl who wins attention without effort.
Maggie can't compete on those terms, and somewhere she knows it.
So the desire to pinch Lucy isn't just jealousy — it's a small, furious rebellion against a system of value that has already decided what kind of girl deserves love.
That's a fascinating frame, Daniel — and it connects directly to how Eliot handles the question of education.
Because we see Tom sent off to school while Maggie is left at home — and what happens to both of them there is extraordinary.
Oliver, you've always had strong feelings about the schoolroom chapters.
Strong feelings is putting it mildly — I think the Tom-at-school chapters are among the funniest and most painful things Eliot ever wrote.
There's a passage where Tom, absolutely crushed by his failures at Latin, decides to pray for academic help.
"And please to make me always remember my Latin."
That sentence — delivered in a low whisper to God after saying his nightly prayers — is devastating and hilarious in equal measure.
And then — and this is what makes Eliot a genius — he has to work out how to pray about Euclid separately.
The comedy of a small boy parsing the theology of mathematical prayer — I defy anyone not to love Tom in that moment.
What moves me equally in that passage is the detail that Tom had been praying for Maggie since she was a baby.
Eliot slips it in as a parenthesis — almost throwaway — but it reframes everything.
This is the same Tom who ignores Maggie, condescends to her, makes her feel small.
And he has been praying for her every night since infancy.
That's the Eliot move — showing you the tenderness inside the rigidity, without excusing the rigidity.
The schoolroom chapters also do something important for our understanding of class and gender working simultaneously.
Tom's humiliation at Mr. Stelling's is an education in the hierarchy of cultural capital — he arrives with the values of a provincial mill-owner's son and is told those values are worthless.
Eliot calls it explicitly: Tom's pride "met with nothing but bruises and crushings."
But here's the irony — Maggie, who is excluded from this education entirely, grasps it more easily than Tom ever does.
Which is the novel's quiet argument about what gets wasted when you deny education to half the population.
And the passage where Maggie gets hold of the Latin Grammar is one of the great comic passages in the novel — I must read a piece of it.

"These mysterious sentences, snatched from an unknown context — like strange horns of beasts, and leaves of unknown plants, brought from some far-off region — gave boundless scope to her imagination."
Strange horns of beasts and leaves of unknown plants — from a Latin grammar!
Maggie turns a textbook into a window onto an entire undiscovered world.
That is the hunger we're talking about — it's not just intellectual, it's almost physical.
And she's proud that she finds it interesting — there's that lovely line, "she was proud because she found it interesting."
Because Tom had said girls couldn't learn Latin — and she's silently refuting him with every page.
There's something both triumphant and heartbreaking about it — she has to prove herself to a standard set by someone who doesn't even notice she's meeting it.
And then there's Philip Wakem — who is, in some ways, the first person in the novel to meet Maggie as an intellectual equal.
Daniel, how do you read their childhood friendship — and what Philip's question to her reveals?
Philip is a fascinating figure because he is simultaneously privileged — the son of the novel's villain — and marked, by his deformity, as outside the social order.
He and Maggie find each other across the lines that are supposed to divide them — class enmity on one side, the stigma of difference on the other.
His question — "if you had had a brother like me, do you think you should have loved him as well as Tom?" — is extraordinary in its vulnerability.
He's asking whether he would be lovable if he were not also the enemy's son — whether the deformity alone would bar him from belonging.
And then there's what Philip says later — which I find almost unbearable in its sweetness.
"I'm very fond of you, Maggie; I shall never forget you.
And when I'm very unhappy, I shall always think of you, and wish I had a sister with dark eyes, just like yours."
A sister with dark eyes, just like yours.
That is a declaration of love from a child who doesn't yet have the word for it.
And it plants a seed in the novel that will flower, and eventually devastate.
What I love is how Maggie responds to the whole encounter.
She decides the way to prove she doesn't mind his deformity is to offer to kiss him as she kisses Tom.
"Should you like me to kiss you, as I do Tom? I will, if you like."
It's the most perfectly Maggie thing in the world — generous, slightly awkward, entirely sincere.
She solves the problem of human connection the way she solves the Latin grammar — with total directness and no social grace whatsoever.
And that gesture — offering the kiss of siblinghood — is Maggie trying to create the world she doesn't have.
Tom won't give her the intellectual companionship she needs, so she finds it in Philip.
Tom won't accept her as an equal — so she offers the only equality she knows how to offer, the equality of affection.
And the tragedy the novel is setting up — patiently, even then — is that none of these substitutions will be enough.
A hunger the world is not equipped to satisfy — and that, I think, is precisely where we've arrived.
Maggie as a child is already, as Daniel says, inventing substitutions — for love, for education, for the brother who keeps letting her down.
When we come back, we'll follow Maggie into adulthood — and ask what the novel makes of the choices she faces when the substitutions run out.

segments.title: Trade and Ruin: The Tulliver Collapse

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've spent time with the Tullivers at home, in the schoolroom, on the river.
Now we turn to the catastrophe at the heart of the novel: the ruin of the family.
How does Eliot build toward financial collapse — and what does that collapse reveal about law, class, education, and the family itself?
Oliver Trevelyan has been waiting, I think, to get his hands on Wakem.
Daniel Rosen sees the legal system as something far more sinister than mere backdrop.
And Caroline Woodcourt knows exactly the moment this segment is building toward — when Maggie tells Tom everything.
The Wakem passages are some of the funniest, most precisely vicious writing in the whole novel.
Eliot gives us Tulliver's hatred of this man in all its irrational glory — and it is glorious.
Listen to how she renders his voice when he thinks about Wakem.
"A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool as a cucumber,—always looking so sure of his game!"
That is pure free indirect discourse — Eliot inhabiting Tulliver's contempt so completely you can hear him spluttering.
And what makes it funnier still is his grievance that his own lawyer, Gore, is insufficiently sinister.
Gore is merely a bald round-featured man with bland manners and fat hands — a profound disappointment.
It's funny, yes — but it's also a very precise anatomy of how a man like Tulliver actually understands the law.
Eliot doesn't let him off with ignorance. She gives him a philosophy.
And it's a philosophy that tells us everything about what the legal system actually is in this world.
The narrator sets it out with devastating clarity.
"Law was a sort of cock-fight, in which it was the business of injured honesty to get a game bird with the best pluck and the strongest spurs."
Injured honesty — that phrase does so much work.
Tulliver is genuinely honest. Eliot never denies him that.
But the system requires him to employ knaves — and he knows it, and proceeds anyway.
That is the trap the novel describes: not individual wickedness, but structural corruption that honest men must participate in to survive.
What stays with me about this whole section is Eliot's treatment of Mrs Tulliver.
She's so often played purely for comedy — the flustered, ineffectual wife.
But Eliot gives her a curious, double-edged sort of influence.
The narrator says her pleading against law had its share of force —
"it might even be comparable to that proverbial feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel's back."
And then Eliot pivots immediately — the blame lies with the previous weight of feathers.
Mrs Tulliver isn't the cause of this disaster. She's just the last straw on a back already breaking.
That's not comedy — that's a quietly devastating judgment on how women get blamed for the catastrophes men create.
Caroline is absolutely right — and there's a further twist there that I love.
When Tulliver hears his wife object, he doesn't hear her — he hears the Dodsons.
She becomes a cipher for everything he resents in her family — and that resentment propels him forward rather than stopping him.
So her opposition — her attempt to prevent ruin — actually accelerates it.
It's a brilliant piece of domestic tragedy dressed up in comic clothing.
And then there's the school. The question of education sits right at the centre of this collapse.
Tulliver sends Tom to Stelling because he wants his son to get on — because he believes education is the route out of vulnerability.
And what does he get? A clergyman with narrow intellects and large wants, as Eliot puts it.
Eliot is scathing about the systemic failure here — and she's specific about why it happens.

"Any of those low callings in which men are obliged to do good work at a low price were forbidden to clergymen; was it their fault if their only resource was to turn out very poor work at a high price?"
The irony is deployed like a scalpel.
The institution of the Church, the institution of the law — both operate on the same logic: poor service extracted at great cost from those who have no alternative.
Tulliver is being squeezed from every direction, and every direction has a respectable name.
All of which makes the scene where Maggie tells Tom absolutely devastating.
Eliot has spent so many pages building the weight of what is about to fall.
And then it arrives in one short sentence — one of the most piercing in the novel.
"Oh, Tom, he will lose the mill and the land and everything; he will have nothing left."
That repetition — the mill, the land, everything, nothing — strips the world bare.
And there's more. Because it isn't only the money.
Maggie then has to tell Tom what has happened to their father — and Eliot renders it with the same terrible plainness.
"He fell off his horse. He has known nobody but me ever since—he seems to have lost his senses."
The ruin is financial. But it is also, in that moment, bodily and spiritual.
That passage is almost impossible to read aloud without your voice catching.
What Eliot does is give Maggie the burden of the telling — a child carrying news too large for a child.
And the words burst from her — that's Eliot's own phrase: the words would burst from her.
All that satirical machinery — the Dodsons, Wakem, the cock-fight of law — it leads here.
To a girl telling her brother their father has lost everything and lost his mind.
Eliot earns every syllable of it.
The satirical and the tragic held in the same hand — that's the peculiar genius of this novel.
We've seen how law, education, marriage, and money conspire against the Tullivers — each institution failing them in its own respectable way.
In our next segment, we'll follow Maggie herself — how she responds to this ruin, and what it demands of her.

segments.title: Brother and Sister: The Fracture Widens

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've been tracing the novel's great central relationship — Tom and Maggie Tulliver — and now we arrive at the forces pulling them apart.
Tom is sent away to school, and what happens there shapes him — and shapes the distance between the siblings — in ways the novel never lets us forget.
Oliver Trevelyan is here — actor, narrator of more classic novels than most of us have read — and he's going to take us straight into the schoolroom.
Daniel Rosen reads Eliot as an anatomist of class power — and education, in this novel, is very much a class instrument.
And Caroline Woodcourt, whose close reading of this novel goes back decades, is here for the emotional grain of these passages.
Oliver — Mr Stelling has entered the story. What do we make of him?
Mr Stelling is one of Eliot's great comic monsters — and she dispatches him with such elegant cruelty.
The whole beaver passage is a masterclass in satirical compression.
She gives us this absurd image — Mr Broderip's beaver building a dam in a London room three flights up, industriously, pointlessly — and then she pivots.
Listen to how she makes the turn:
"With the same unerring instinct Mr Stelling set to work at his natural method of instilling the Eton Grammar and Euclid into the mind of Tom Tulliver."
That word "instilling" — she means pouring liquid into a vessel, of course — and poor Tom is a vessel that simply cannot receive this particular liquid.
The comedy is perfect, but there's a boy suffering inside it.
And the comedy is doing serious ideological work.
Stelling's conviction that the Eton Grammar is the only basis of solid instruction — that everything else produces mere smatterers — is not personal eccentricity.
It is the entire apparatus of class reproduction dressed up as pedagogy.
Eliot is precise about what Stelling actually believes in — and it's a telling list.
"He thought religion was a very excellent thing, and Aristotle a great authority, and deaneries and prebends useful institutions, and Great Britain the providential bulwark of Protestantism."
Deaneries and prebends — those are Church sinecures, income without labour — sitting right beside Aristotle and Great Britain.
Eliot has quietly shown us that the entire edifice — classical education, religion, patriotism — is a system of mutual protection for men like Stelling.
Tom Tulliver is simply the raw material that system does not know what to do with.
What moves me in the next passage is that Eliot refuses to let the satire swallow the boy whole.
She stops and lists what Tom can actually do — what his intelligence looks like when no one is measuring it wrongly.
He can predict how many horses are cantering behind him. He can throw a stone into the centre of a given ripple. He can draw near-perfect squares freehand.
These are things a child notices about the world when the world is actually interesting to them.
And then Eliot performs this extraordinary rhetorical move — the metaphor passage — and she aims it directly at Stelling and his kind.

"O Aristotle! if you had had the advantage of being 'the freshest modern' instead of the greatest ancient, would you not have mingled your praise of metaphorical speech, as a sign of high intelligence, with a lamentation that intelligence so rarely shows itself in speech without metaphor."
She's turning the weapons of classical education — Aristotle himself — against the men who wield them so bluntly.
It's a gorgeous piece of ventriloquism — she invokes Aristotle to undercut the Aristotelians.
And then comes Philip Wakem — which changes everything.
Tom's first encounter with Philip is extraordinary because Eliot shows us Tom's mind working in real time — prejudice, curiosity, grudging fascination.
He notices Philip's face is not disagreeable. Then he notices the hump and reaches for an explanation.
And Eliot gives us this perfectly calibrated detail — almost a throwaway — that lands like a small bomb.

"There was a humpbacked tailor in the neighbourhood of Mr Jacobs's academy, who was considered a very unamiable character, and was much hooted after by public-spirited boys solely on the ground of his unsatisfactory moral qualities."
"Public-spirited boys." "Unsatisfactory moral qualities." She's skewering the rationalisation of cruelty with three words apiece.
Tom's cruelty toward Philip is not simply boyish thoughtlessness — it is class ideology internalised by a child who is himself its victim.
Tom has absorbed from his father's hot-breathed speeches that Wakem means rascality, that deformity and moral corruption are linked.
He is a miller's son being educated above his class, surrounded by the values of that class, and he has nowhere to put his own dispossession except outward — onto Philip.
But Eliot doesn't let Tom off the hook, and she doesn't sentimentalise Philip either.
Philip's wish to have been a Greek hero — to have fought and written tragedies and died grandly like Socrates — is affecting, yes.

"I should like to have been a Greek and fought the Persians, and then have come home and have written tragedies, or else have been listened to by everybody for my wisdom, like Socrates, and have died a grand death."
But Eliot adds — in parentheses, which is her most quietly devastating register — that Philip is not without a wish to impress the well-made barbarian with a sense of his mental superiority.
These two boys are already measuring each other — and the measuring is already entangled with pain.
And underneath all of this schoolroom comedy and cruelty, the novel keeps returning to what it costs Mr Tulliver — what it costs the father.
There is a moment — just a single line of dialogue — that I find almost unbearable.
Maggie is with him. She loves him utterly. He knows it.
And he says, very simply:
"Ay, my little wench, but I shall never live twice o'er."
That is everything. Her love, his love for her — and the fact that none of it gives him back what's gone.
The schoolroom passages, the education satire — they are building toward this.
The wrong education, the wrong school, the debt, the ruin — it all flows from choices made when life could still be redirected.
But you cannot live twice o'er.
That line sits with you.
A father's grief measured not in loss of money but in the irreversibility of time.
Oliver, Daniel, Caroline — thank you for everything you've brought to this schoolroom today.
In our next segment, we turn to the Dodson aunts — and the iron laws of respectability that press down on this family from a very different angle.

segments.title: A Provincial Tragedy: Comedy and Constraint

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.

I'm your host, and over the course of this episode we're going to spend time inside one of the great English novels — a book about memory, family, class, and what it costs to be born the wrong person in the wrong place.
Today's segment is called A Provincial Tragedy: Comedy and Constraint — because George Eliot's genius is that she makes you laugh before she breaks your heart.
Three brilliant readers are with me today, and I want to introduce them properly.
Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more classic novels than anyone alive, and he reads George Eliot the way a musician reads a score — hearing every rest and every crescendo.
Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as X-rays of class power — he finds the machinery underneath the sentiment.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since adolescence and brings to it the kind of love that is also argument.
Oliver, let's begin with the novel's opening move — because it is, I think, one of the most quietly audacious openings in Victorian fiction.
Audacious is exactly right, and I'd go further — it's a conjuring trick performed in plain sight.
Eliot opens the novel in what feels like a present tense reverie — we're watching the mill, watching the river, watching young Maggie.
And then she pulls the rug.
She says — and I must read this because the sentence is everything —

"Ah, my arms are really benumbed. I have been pressing my elbows on the arms of my chair, and dreaming that I was standing on the bridge in front of Dorlcote Mill, as it looked one February afternoon many years ago."
She was asleep in a chair the whole time.
Everything we thought we saw — the mill, the river, the child — was memory inside a dream inside a novel.
The whole book is announced in that one moment of waking up with numb arms.
What gets me about that passage is the physical comedy of it.
The numb arms.
This is a novelist who has just built the most gorgeous, atmospheric opening — the river, the light, the child on the bank — and she punctures it with numb arms.
It tells you immediately that this narrator is self-aware and a little rueful — she's nostalgic, but she's not going to let nostalgia become indulgence.
And then she says she was going to tell us what Mr and Mrs Tulliver were talking about — as if she'd merely wandered off topic for a moment.
The breezy confidence of that is wonderful.
There's something more unsettling underneath that breeziness, though.
The novel is written from a future in which everything we're about to encounter is already gone.
The mill is already a ruin in memory before we've even met the Tullivers.
That's not just a narrative device — it's a statement about how class dispossession works.
The world these people built and belonged to is always already being taken from them.
Daniel, that's true — and it makes the comedy that follows feel more precious, not less.
Because if you know the house is coming down, you want to spend every possible moment inside it while it still stands.
And Eliot gives us a lot of time inside.
She gives us, for instance, the magnificent Reverend Stelling — a man who intends to be great and is, in fact, merely large.
Listen to this —
"A clergyman who has such vigorous intentions naturally gets a little into debt at starting."
That word — naturally.
Eliot tucks the entire critique of clerical ambition into one ironic adverb.
The Stelling portrait is so dense with satirical detail it almost makes you dizzy.
His doctrine was of no particular school — it had a tinge of evangelicalism because that was the telling thing just then in the diocese.
The man has calibrated his very theology to the market.
And he intends to edit a Greek play — he hasn't yet selected which one, mind you — while also attending to Mrs Stelling.
There is something so pitifully human in that detail.
He's a fraud, but he's a busy fraud — and Eliot won't let him be simply monstrous.
Stelling isn't anomalous, though — that's what Eliot insists on.
He is the system functioning correctly.
The Church, the school, the patronage networks — all of it rewards exactly the combination of bluster and social ambition that Stelling embodies.
He has no interest beyond a problematic relationship to a great lawyer who had not yet become Lord Chancellor — Eliot is very precise about the flimsiness of his connections.
And yet he will rise, and Tom Tulliver will pay the price for being educated by him.
The comedy and the injustice are not separable.
And yet Tom himself — young Tom — is also a kind of comic creation.
There's a passage with him and Bob Jakin that I find completely irresistible.
Tom imagines building a boat in the event of a great flood — and it's wonderful because it is simultaneously generous and magnificently self-important.
"When I'm a man, I shall make a boat with a wooden house on the top of it, like Noah's ark, and keep plenty to eat in it,—rabbits and things,—all ready."
And then — the beneficent condescension of the final line — he tells Bob he would take him in if he saw him swimming.
In the tone, Eliot says, of a benevolent patron.
Tom is nine years old and he is already performing the role of a great man toward his social inferiors.
I love that passage, but it makes me sad too.
Because Tom's imagination is genuinely alive there — the rabbits, the wooden house, the all ready — there's such delight in the specificity.
And yet Eliot frames it with that tiny phrase — benevolent patron — which is both funny and already a verdict on who Tom is going to become.
The child is father to the man, and not always in a flattering way.
And Bob Jakin would be swimming, of course — because Bob has nothing.
Tom imagines the flood as an adventure, a test of his future competence.
For Bob, the flood — and this is a novel where the flood is real — is simply annihilation.
The class difference is there even in how they're allowed to imagine disaster.
Before we move on, I want to bring us to a scene that is, for me, the great hinge of the childhood section.
Tom is showing off with a sword — as boys do — and it falls on his foot.
He faints.
And Maggie — who thinks he is dead — shakes him by the collar.
Shakes him, as if that would bring him back to life.
And then this —
"She couldn't sorrow yet that he had hurt his foot; it seemed as if all happiness lay in his being alive."
The comedy of the situation — the showboating, the faint — falls completely away.
What's left is just Maggie's love — absolute, wordless, and already painful.
That sentence stops me every time.
She couldn't sorrow yet — yet.
That single word contains the whole of Maggie's future — the sorrow will come, the full reckoning will come, but in this moment all that matters is that he is breathing.
Eliot is doing something very precise about the hierarchy of feelings — how relief can be so total it temporarily erases everything else.
It's also notable that Mr Stelling is the first adult on the scene.
He comes down from his upstairs study — from his study, where he is presumably planning his great Greek edition.
And he finds two children on the floor — one unconscious, one wild-eyed and screaming.
The man who is going to shape Tom's education — whose negligence and vanity will leave Tom ill-equipped for life — he is just getting there.
Always just arriving after the damage is done.
What strikes me listening to all three of you is that this novel refuses to keep its registers separate.
The satire of Stelling, the tenderness of Maggie shaking Tom, the sly comedy of the numb arms — they're all part of the same breath.
In a moment, we'll turn to what happens when that provincial world begins to crack — when the comedy cedes to something harder and more irreversible.
Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've been circling the novel's emotional heart, and now we move to something that runs beneath everything in this book — the question of judgment.
Who gets to judge whom, on what grounds, and at what cost.
Daniel Rosen has been looking hard at the passages where Eliot turns her analytical eye on Tom Tulliver — and on the society that produces him.
Daniel is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of power — and few novels repay that reading more richly than this one.
Oliver Trevelyan joins us as ever — the man who has read more classic novels aloud than any human being alive, and who will, I suspect, have strong feelings about Maggie's great speech.
And Caroline Woodcourt is here — the critic who came to this novel as a teenager and has never quite recovered, which is the highest possible recommendation.
Daniel — let's begin with Tom Tulliver.
Because Eliot does something quite startling in her very first physical description of him — she uses his ordinary face as a kind of trap.
Yes — and it's one of the most quietly devastating moves in the novel's opening chapters.
Eliot describes Tom as one of those lads that grow everywhere in England — interchangeable, generic, cream-and-roses.
And against that, poor Maggie's face — which Nature seemed to have moulded and coloured with the most decided intention.
The social reading almost writes itself: Maggie is legible, marked, scrutinised — and Tom is invisible in his normativity.
But then Eliot springs the trap.
She writes — and this is the passage I keep returning to:
"Under these average boyish physiognomies that she seems to turn off by the gross, she conceals some of her most rigid, inflexible purposes, some of her most unmodifiable characters."
The ordinariness is not innocence — it is cover.
Tom's blankness is the face that power wears when it doesn't need to explain itself.
What strikes me every time I read that passage is the word "gross" — she seems to turn them off by the gross.
It's a manufacturing term — bulk production.
Nature herself running a factory line of Tom Tullivers.
And the comedy of it is very Eliotic — the satirical edge is so sharp you almost miss it the first time.
But by the time Tom is confronting Maggie in the Red Deeps, you understand exactly what that unmodifiable character means in practice.
It means a conscience that cannot be questioned — by anyone, including himself.
And Eliot is absolutely pitiless on that point — pitiless in the most compassionate way.
She gives us the inside of Tom's head, and what we find there is not cruelty exactly — it's something worse.
There's that extraordinary sentence about his motives — let me find it precisely because it deserves to be heard exactly:

"Tom was not given to inquire subtly into his own motives any more than into other matters of an intangible kind; he was quite sure that his own motives as well as actions were good, else he would have had nothing to do with them."
That last clause — else he would have had nothing to do with them.
It's almost a joke — but it's the most terrifying joke in the novel.
He has built a perfect moral tautology, and he lives inside it without a crack.
That's exactly right — and what Eliot shows is that Tom's certainty is not incidental to his social position, it is constituted by it.
The man who inherits the right to judge does not need to examine his judgments.
And Eliot connects this, I think, directly to the novel's great passage on the man of maxims — in Chapter 55.
The narrator argues — and she argues it as a proposition, not as a dramatic scene — that moral judgment guided purely by general rules is a kind of ethical violence.
She writes:

"the mysterious complexity of our life is not to be embraced by maxims, and that to lace ourselves up in formulas of that sort is to repress all the divine promptings and inspirations that spring from growing insight and sympathy."
Lace ourselves up — that's the image she chooses.
Not a shield, not a fortress — a corset.
Something tight, gendered, worn against the body — and entirely self-imposed.
And then there is Maggie's own answer to Tom — which is the moment the novel burns brightest, I think.
She has been held in silence for so long — the good sister, the dutiful daughter, writhing under Tom's verdict — and then it breaks.
She says — and I want to read this fully, because half-quoting it would be a betrayal:
"You have no pity; you have no sense of your own imperfection and your own sins. It is a sin to be hard; it is not fitting for a mortal, for a Christian.
You are nothing but a Pharisee. You thank God for nothing but your own virtues; you think they are great enough to win you everything else.
You have not even a vision of feelings by the side of which your shining virtues are mere darkness!"
Your shining virtues are mere darkness.
I have read that sentence perhaps thirty times and it still makes me catch my breath.
When I read that passage aloud — and I have, many times — the challenge is not to oversell it.
Because the vehemence is already there — Eliot marks it explicitly, still with vehemence, she says.
A performer's job is to trust the text.
What gets me is the theological reach of it — Maggie isn't just calling Tom unkind, she's calling him spiritually blind.
A Pharisee — someone whose righteousness is real and legible and entirely beside the point.
And the tragedy is that Tom cannot hear it — because the man described by that speech cannot, by definition, recognise himself in it.
Which brings us, finally, to the scene I find most unbearable in the entire novel — Tulliver at the end.
When he is broken — financially, physically, morally broken — and he turns to his wife and says simply:
"Give me a kiss, Bessy, and let us bear one another no ill-will; we shall never be young again—this world's been too many for me."
This world's been too many for me.
Six words that contain the entire verdict on everything the novel has shown us about property, law, debt, and social belonging.
Tulliver is not a radical — he never questions the system that destroys him.
And that is precisely what makes the line so devastating — the defeated man who cannot name what defeated him.
This world's been too many for me — there is something in that line that sits beside you long after you close the book.
We've moved from the factory line of boyish faces to Maggie's great accusation to a father's final surrender, and what connects all of it is this question of who sees clearly and at what price.
In our next segment, we're going to look at the world Maggie inherits — the St. Ogg's society that judges her, and what Eliot thinks of those judges.

segments.title: Closing: The Flood and What It Takes

utterances.text: We've arrived at the end of our journey through The Mill on the Floss — and the novel itself ends in water.
The flood that takes Maggie and Tom together is one of the most contested endings in Victorian fiction.
But before we get there, I want to spend a little time with what George Eliot has been building all along — the moral architecture of this novel.
Duty, renunciation, faithfulness — these are not abstract ideals here. They are pressed against real flesh, real longing.
Caroline, I want to start with you on Maggie's great declaration to Stephen — the moment when she articulates what faithfulness actually means.
That speech to Stephen is — for me — the emotional and moral centre of the entire novel.
It's Maggie at her most lucid and her most anguished, simultaneously.
She says something that almost sounds like a formula — but listen to the weight beneath it.
"Faithfulness and constancy mean something else besides doing what is easiest and pleasantest to ourselves."
"They mean renouncing whatever is opposed to the reliance others have in us."
The word she chooses is reliance. Not love. Not affection. Reliance.
People have built their lives on the assumption that Maggie is trustworthy. And she knows it.
What wrecks you is the line about Lucy: 'She believed in me — she loved me — she was so good to me.'
Caroline is right that the word reliance does tremendous work in that passage.
But what strikes me as a performer is the rhythm of Maggie's self-accusation — the way it accelerates and then breaks.
She says she should have prayed more, rushed away — and then suddenly she stops arguing and just says: 'Oh, what is Lucy feeling now?'
The theory collapses into a person. The ethics collapse into a face.
That is George Eliot's genius — she never lets the moral framework float free of the actual human being who suffers inside it.
I want to press on that a little — because the novel is deeply ambivalent about whether Maggie's renunciation is heroic or tragic or simply enforced.
A woman in Maggie's position has almost nothing. No profession, no independent income, no standing.
Her entire social existence depends on being considered good — trustworthy, as Caroline said.
So when Maggie renounces Stephen and invokes faithfulness, I hear that as partly genuine moral feeling — and partly the only option available to her.
But I think George Eliot gives us a counter-portrait — and that's Lucy Deane.
There's a passage where Lucy is walking up and down after Stephen's goodbye — just glowing — and simultaneously thinking about Maggie's room.

"Even now, her mind, with that instantaneous alternation which makes two currents of feeling or imagination seem simultaneous, is glancing continually from Stephen to the preparations she has only half finished in Maggie's room."
Lucy is the character who manages to hold self-interest and genuine love together without the seams showing.
And what the novel implies — quietly, devastatingly — is that Maggie cannot do that. The world will not allow it.
The Lucy passage is one I return to again and again — the narrator's voice there is so mischievously affectionate.
George Eliot says Lucy's 'small egoisms were impregnated' with benevolence — which is a wonderfully double-edged compliment.
But Daniel's point cuts deep. Lucy can afford to be generous because she is safe.
She has standing, she has love, she has a father who adores her. Maggie has none of that security.
And yet — and this is what undoes me — Maggie loves Lucy back with something quite close to the same generosity.
Can I bring us back to something that I think underpins all of this — Eliot's defence of childhood pain?
There's a passage early in the novel — when young Maggie has cut her hair off in a rage and is sitting, ruined, among her locks — that the narrator turns into a full philosophical manifesto.
She compares Maggie — and I love this — to Ajax among the slaughtered sheep. Amid a disaster of her own making.
And then Eliot makes her argument. Listen to this.
"Very trivial, perhaps, this anguish seems to weather-worn mortals who have to think of Christmas bills, dead loves, and broken friendships."
"But it was not less bitter to Maggie — perhaps it was even more bitter — than what we are fond of calling antithetically the real troubles of mature life."
'The real troubles of mature life.' She puts that in inverted commas — in her mind if not on the page — and absolutely refuses the condescension.
That argument is the seed of the entire novel. If you don't believe Maggie's childhood suffering was real, you can't believe in the flood.
That's exactly right — and what makes that passage politically sharp as well as philosophically generous is the contrast with Tom.
Eliot notes that Tom never made the same kind of foolish mistakes Maggie did — he had an instinctive discernment of what would serve his advantage.
And when Tom did err, he simply refused remorse. He espoused his mistake. He 'didn't mind.'
This is the psychological template for everything that follows. Tom is equipped for the world as it is. Maggie is equipped for a world that doesn't exist yet.
The flood doesn't feel arbitrary to me. It feels like the only exit George Eliot could find for a character the world had no place for.
And yet there's that moment of reconciliation in the boat — Maggie rowing toward Tom, Tom finally seeing her clearly.
George Eliot gives them that. Seconds, perhaps, but she gives them that.
It doesn't redeem the world's cruelty. But it redeems something — the childhood they shared, maybe.
All those early scenes — the mill, the attic, the jam puff, Maggie sitting among her cut hair — they have been leading here.
Eliot made us feel the weight of those years. So the loss of them is insupportable.
Oliver, a last word — what does the novel finally ask of us as readers?
I think it asks us to resist exactly the condescension that passage warns against.
George Eliot's narrator says we look on at the troubles of children with a 'smiling disbelief in the reality of their pain.'
The Mill on the Floss is a four-hundred-page argument against that smile.
It insists that Maggie's pain — from the very first chapter to the last — was real, was legitimate, and mattered.
And if we finish the novel believing that, George Eliot has done her work.
Thank you to Oliver Trevelyan, Daniel Rosen, and Caroline Woodcourt — and to you for listening to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.

c11:p0.text:
Maggie’s intentions, as usual, were on a larger scale than Tom imagined.
The resolution that gathered in her mind, after Tom and Lucy had walked away,
was not so simple as that of going home. No! she would run away and go to the
gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more. That was by no means a new idea
to Maggie; she had been so often told she was like a gypsy, and “half
wild,” that when she was miserable it seemed to her the only way of
escaping opprobrium, and being entirely in harmony with circumstances, would be
to live in a little brown tent on the commons; the gypsies, she considered,
would gladly receive her and pay her much respect on account of her superior
knowledge. She had once mentioned her views on this point to Tom and suggested
that he should stain his face brown, and they should run away together; but Tom
rejected the scheme with contempt, observing that gypsies were thieves, and
hardly got anything to eat and had nothing to drive but a donkey. To-day
however, Maggie thought her misery had reached a pitch at which gypsydom was
her refuge, and she rose from her seat on the roots of the tree with the sense
that this was a great crisis in her life; she would run straight away till she
came to Dunlow Common, where there would certainly be gypsies; and cruel Tom,
and the rest of her relations who found fault with her, should never see her
any more. She thought of her father as she ran along, but she reconciled
herself to the idea of parting with him, by determining that she would secretly
send him a letter by a small gypsy, who would run away without telling where
she was, and just let him know that she was well and happy, and always loved
him very much.
c11:p0.summary: Maggie resolves to run away to the gypsies after Tom's rejection, a fantasy she has long harboured as a way to escape family reproach and find harmony with her perceived wild nature.
c11:p0.best_quote: No! she would run away and go to the gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more.

c11:p34.text:
Maggie Tulliver, you perceive, was by no means that well trained, well-informed
young person that a small female of eight or nine necessarily is in these days;
she had only been to school a year at St Ogg’s, and had so few books
that she sometimes read the dictionary; so that in travelling over her small
mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected
knowledge. She could have informed you that there was such a word as
“polygamy,” and being also acquainted with
“polysyllable,” she had deduced the conclusion that
“poly” mean “many”; but she had had no idea that
gypsies were not well supplied with groceries, and her thoughts generally were
the oddest mixture of clear-eyed acumen and blind dreams.
c11:p34.summary: The narrator reflects on Maggie's unusual, self-taught education: sophisticated in etymology and moral philosophy but naive about practical realities.
c11:p34.best_quote: in travelling over her small mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge.

c11:p35.text:
Her ideas about the gypsies had undergone a rapid modification in the last five
minutes. From having considered them very respectful companions, amenable to
instruction, she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon
as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking; the suspicion crossed
her that the fierce-eyed old man was in fact the Devil, who might drop that
transparent disguise at any moment, and turn either into the grinning
blacksmith, or else a fiery-eyed monster with dragon’s wings. It was no
use trying to eat the stew, and yet the thing she most dreaded was to offend
the gypsies, by betraying her extremely unfavourable opinion of them; and she
wondered, with a keenness of interest that no theologian could have exceeded,
whether, if the Devil were really present, he would know her thoughts.
c11:p35.summary: Maggie's fantasy collapses into paranoid horror as she imagines the gypsies as cannibals and the fierce-eyed man as the Devil.
c11:p35.best_quote: she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking.

c10:p1.text:
Maggie said nothing, but turned away from her with a deeper frown. As long as
Tom seemed to prefer Lucy to her, Lucy made part of his unkindness. Maggie
would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty
little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse; but
then, Tom had always been quite indifferent to Lucy before, and it had been
left to Maggie to pet and make much of her. As it was, she was actually
beginning to think that she should like to make Lucy cry by slapping or
pinching her, especially as it might vex Tom, whom it was of no use to slap,
even if she dared, because he didn’t mind it. And if Lucy hadn’t
been there, Maggie was sure he would have got friends with her sooner.
c10:p1.summary: Maggie's jealousy transforms her affection into potential cruelty; she blames Lucy for Tom's unkindness and fantasizes about hurting her to vex Tom.
c10:p1.best_quote: Maggie would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse; but then, Tom had always been quite indifferent to Lucy before, and it had been left to Maggie to pet and make much of her.

c14:p11.text:
Yet, strange to say, under this vigorous treatment Tom became more like a girl
than he had ever been in his life before. He had a large share of pride, which
had hitherto found itself very comfortable in the world, despising Old Goggles,
and reposing in the sense of unquestioned rights; but now this same pride met
with nothing but bruises and crushings. Tom was too clear-sighted not to be
aware that Mr Stelling’s standard of things was quite different, was
certainly something higher in the eyes of the world than that of the people he
had been living amongst, and that, brought in contact with it, he, Tom
Tulliver, appeared uncouth and stupid; he was by no means indifferent to this,
and his pride got into an uneasy condition which quite nullified his boyish
self-satisfaction, and gave him something of the girl’s susceptibility.
He was of a very firm, not to say obstinate, disposition, but there was no
brute-like rebellion and recklessness in his nature; the human sensibilities
predominated, and if it had occurred to him that he could enable himself to
show some quickness at his lessons, and so acquire Mr Stelling’s
approbation, by standing on one leg for an inconvenient length of time, or
rapping his head moderately against the wall, or any voluntary action of that
sort, he would certainly have tried it. But no; Tom had never heard that these
measures would brighten the understanding, or strengthen the verbal memory; and
he was not given to hypothesis and experiment. It did occur to him that he
could perhaps get some help by praying for it; but as the prayers he said every
evening were forms learned by heart, he rather shrank from the novelty and
irregularity of introducing an extempore passage on a topic of petition for
which he was not aware of any precedent. But one day, when he had broken down,
for the fifth time, in the supines of the third conjugation, and Mr Stelling,
convinced that this must be carelessness, since it transcended the bounds of
possible stupidity, had lectured him very seriously, pointing out that if he
failed to seize the present golden opportunity of learning supines, he would
have to regret it when he became a man,—Tom, more miserable than usual,
determined to try his sole resource; and that evening, after his usual form of
prayer for his parents and “little sister” (he had begun to pray
for Maggie when she was a baby), and that he might be able always to keep
God’s commandments, he added, in the same low whisper, “and please
to make me always remember my Latin.” He paused a little to consider how
he should pray about Euclid—whether he should ask to see what it meant,
or whether there was any other mental state which would be more applicable to
the case. But at last he added: “And make Mr Stelling say I
sha’n’t do Euclid any more. Amen.”
c14:p11.summary: Humiliated by repeated failures, Tom resorts to prayer, adding petitions for Latin and Euclid to his nightly prayers, showing his desperation and underlying sensitivity.
c14:p11.best_quote: and please to make me always remember my Latin

c14:p58.text:
Maggie found the Latin Grammar quite soothing after her mathematical
mortification; for she delighted in new words, and quickly found that there was
an English Key at the end, which would make her very wise about Latin, at
slight expense. She presently made up her mind to skip the rules in the Syntax,
the examples became so absorbing. These mysterious sentences, snatched from an
unknown context,—like strange horns of beasts, and leaves of unknown
plants, brought from some far-off region,—gave boundless scope to her
imagination, and were all the more fascinating because they were in a peculiar
tongue of their own, which she could learn to interpret. It was really very
interesting, the Latin Grammar that Tom had said no girls could learn; and she
was proud because she found it interesting. The most fragmentary examples were
her favourites.  Mors omnibus est communis  would have been jejune, only
she liked to know the Latin; but the fortunate gentleman whom every one
congratulated because he had a son “endowed with  such  a
disposition” afforded her a great deal of pleasant conjecture, and she
was quite lost in the “thick grove penetrable by no star,” when Tom
called out,—
c14:p58.summary: Maggie discovers joy in the Latin Grammar's fragmentary examples, finding them imaginatively stimulating and delighting in the foreign language's mysterious beauty.
c14:p58.best_quote: These mysterious sentences, snatched from an unknown context,—like strange horns of beasts, and leaves of unknown plants, brought from some far-off region,—gave boundless scope to her imagination

c19:p18.text:
“It’s about Philoctetes, the lame man I was telling you of
yesterday,” he answered, resting his head on his hand, and looking at her
as if he were not at all sorry to be interrupted. Maggie, in her absent way,
continued to lean forward, resting on her arms and moving her feet about, while
her dark eyes got more and more fixed and vacant, as if she had quite forgotten
Philip and his book.
c19:p18.summary: Philip asks whether Maggie would love him as well as Tom if he were her brother, a question laden with the subtext of his physical deformity and desire for affection.
c19:p18.best_quote: Maggie, if you had had a brother like me, do you think you should have loved him as well as Tom?

c19:p27.text: “Oh, yes, I should think so,” said Maggie, laughing.
c19:p27.summary: Philip confesses his deep and enduring affection for Maggie, stating he will remember her always and, in unhappiness, will think of her and wish for a sister with her dark eyes.
c19:p27.best_quote: I'm very fond of you, Maggie; I shall never forget you. And when I'm very unhappy, I shall always think of you, and wish I had a sister with dark eyes, just like yours.

c19:p31.text:
“Why, I think you’re fonder of me than Tom is,” said Maggie,
rather sorrowfully. Then, wondering how she could convince Philip that she
could like him just as well, although he was crooked, she said:
c19:p31.summary: Wondering how to demonstrate that she can love Philip despite his deformity, Maggie offers to kiss him as she kisses her brother Tom.
c19:p31.best_quote: Should you like me to kiss you, as I do Tom? I will, if you like.

c15:p19.text:
But not even a direct argument from that typical Dodson female herself against
his going to law could have heightened his disposition toward it so much as the
mere thought of Wakem, continually freshened by the sight of the too able
attorney on market-days. Wakem, to his certain knowledge, was (metaphorically
speaking) at the bottom of Pivart’s irrigation; Wakem had tried to make
Dix stand out, and go to law about the dam; it was unquestionably Wakem who had
caused Mr Tulliver to lose the suit about the right of road and the bridge
that made a thoroughfare of his land for every vagabond who preferred an
opportunity of damaging private property to walking like an honest man along
the highroad; all lawyers were more or less rascals, but Wakem’s
rascality was of that peculiarly aggravated kind which placed itself in
opposition to that form of right embodied in Mr Tulliver’s interests and
opinions. And as an extra touch of bitterness, the injured miller had recently,
in borrowing the five hundred pounds, been obliged to carry a little business
to Wakem’s office on his own account. A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool
as a cucumber,—always looking so sure of his game! And it was vexatious
that Lawyer Gore was not more like him, but was a bald, round-featured man,
with bland manners and fat hands; a game-cock that you would be rash to bet
upon against Wakem. Gore was a sly fellow. His weakness did not lie on the side
of scrupulosity; but the largest amount of winking, however significant, is not
equivalent to seeing through a stone wall; and confident as Mr Tulliver was in
his principle that water was water, and in the direct inference that Pivart had
not a leg to stand on in this affair of irrigation, he had an uncomfortable
suspicion that Wakem had more law to show against this (rationally)
irrefragable inference than Gore could show for it. But then, if they went to
law, there was a chance for Mr Tulliver to employ Counsellor Wylde on his
side, instead of having that admirable bully against him; and the prospect of
seeing a witness of Wakem’s made to perspire and become confounded, as
Mr Tulliver’s witness had once been, was alluring to the love of
retributive justice.
c15:p19.summary: The narrator details Mr Tulliver's bitter conviction that Wakem orchestrates all his legal troubles and has humiliated him repeatedly; reveals his visceral hatred of the lawyer.
c15:p19.best_quote: A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool as a cucumber,—always looking so sure of his game!

c15:p9.text:
Mr Tulliver was a strictly honest man, and proud of being honest, but he
considered that in law the ends of justice could only be achieved by employing
a stronger knave to frustrate a weaker. Law was a sort of cock-fight, in which
it was the business of injured honesty to get a game bird with the best pluck
and the strongest spurs.
c15:p9.summary: The narrator explains Mr Tulliver's philosophy: he considers himself honest but believes justice in law requires employing a cleverer knave to defeat one's opponent.
c15:p9.best_quote: Law was a sort of cock-fight, in which it was the business of injured honesty to get a game bird with the best pluck and the strongest spurs

c15:p18.text:
Mrs Tulliver, as we have seen, was not without influence over her husband. No
woman is; she can always incline him to do either what she wishes, or the
reverse; and on the composite impulses that were threatening to hurry Mr
Tulliver into “law,” Mrs Tulliver’s monotonous pleading had
doubtless its share of force; it might even be comparable to that proverbial
feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel’s back;
though, on a strictly impartial view, the blame ought rather to lie with the
previous weight of feathers which had already placed the back in such imminent
peril that an otherwise innocent feather could not settle on it without
mischief. Not that Mrs Tulliver’s feeble beseeching could have had this
feather’s weight in virtue of her single personality; but whenever she
departed from entire assent to her husband, he saw in her the representative of
the Dodson family; and it was a guiding principle with Mr Tulliver to let the
Dodsons know that they were not to domineer over  him , or—more
specifically—that a male Tulliver was far more than equal to four female
Dodsons, even though one of them was Mrs Glegg.
c15:p18.summary: The narrator observes that Mrs Tulliver's weak pleading against law has cumulative force when combined with his fear of Dodson influence, though she is not powerful in herself.
c15:p18.best_quote: it might even be comparable to that proverbial feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel's back

c17:p2.text:
All this, you remember, happened in those dark ages when there were no schools
of design; before schoolmasters were invariably men of scrupulous integrity,
and before the clergy were all men of enlarged minds and varied culture. In
those less favoured days, it is no fable that there were other clergymen
besides Mr Stelling who had narrow intellects and large wants, and whose
income, by a logical confusion to which Fortune, being a female as well as
blindfold, is peculiarly liable, was proportioned not to their wants but to
their intellect, with which income has clearly no inherent relation. The
problem these gentlemen had to solve was to readjust the proportion between
their wants and their income; and since wants are not easily starved to death,
the simpler method appeared to be to raise their income. There was but one way
of doing this; any of those low callings in which men are obliged to do good
work at a low price were forbidden to clergymen; was it their fault if their
only resource was to turn out very poor work at a high price? Besides, how
should Mr Stelling be expected to know that education was a delicate and
difficult business, any more than an animal endowed with a power of boring a
hole through a rock should be expected to have wide views of excavation? Mr
Stelling’s faculties had been early trained to boring in a straight line,
and he had no faculty to spare. But among Tom’s contemporaries, whose
fathers cast their sons on clerical instruction to find them ignorant after
many days, there were many far less lucky than Tom Tulliver. Education was
almost entirely a matter of luck—usually of ill-luck—in those
distant days. The state of mind in which you take a billiard-cue or a dice-box
in your hand is one of sober certainty compared with that of old-fashioned
fathers, like Mr Tulliver, when they selected a school or a tutor for their
sons. Excellent men, who had been forced all their lives to spell on an
impromptu-phonetic system, and having carried on a successful business in spite
of this disadvantage, had acquired money enough to give their sons a better
start in life than they had had themselves, must necessarily take their chance
as to the conscience and the competence of the schoolmaster whose circular fell
in their way, and appeared to promise so much more than they would ever have
thought of asking for, including the return of linen, fork, and spoon. It was
happy for them if some ambitious draper of their acquaintance had not brought
up his son to the Church, and if that young gentleman, at the age of
four-and-twenty, had not closed his college dissipations by an imprudent
marriage; otherwise, these innocent fathers, desirous of doing the best for
their offspring, could only escape the draper’s son by happening to be on
the foundation of a grammar-school as yet unvisited by commissioners, where two
or three boys could have, all to themselves, the advantages of a large and
lofty building, together with a head-master, toothless, dim-eyed and deaf,
whose erudite indistinctness and inattention were engrossed by them at the rate
of three hundred pounds a-head,—a ripe scholar, doubtless, when first
appointed; but all ripeness beneath the sun has a further stage less esteemed
in the market.
c17:p2.summary: Eliot reflects on the educational chaos of the pre-reform era, where incompetent clergymen like Mr Stelling ran schools as profit ventures, and anxious fathers had no reliable way to judge the quality of instruction their sons would receive.
c17:p2.best_quote: There was but one way of doing this; any of those low callings in which men are obliged to do good work at a low price were forbidden to clergymen; was it their fault if their only resource was to turn out very poor work at a high price?

c20:p18.text:
“Yes,” said Maggie, again faintly. Then, urged to fuller speech by
Tom’s freedom from apprehension, she said loudly and rapidly, as if the
words  would  burst from her: “Oh, Tom, he will lose the mill and
the land and everything; he will have nothing left.”
c20:p18.summary: Maggie urgently reveals that her father will lose the mill, the land, and everything he owns.
c20:p18.best_quote: Oh, Tom, he will lose the mill and the land and everything; he will have nothing left.

c20:p30.text:
“He’s at home,” said Maggie, finding it easier to reply to
that question. “But,” she added, after a pause, “not
himself—he fell off his horse. He has known nobody but me ever
since—he seems to have lost his senses. O father,
father——”
c20:p30.summary: Maggie reveals that Mr Tulliver fell from his horse and has lost consciousness since the accident, recognizing no one but Maggie.
c20:p30.best_quote: He's at home. But he fell off his horse. He has known nobody but me ever since—he seems to have lost his senses.

c14:p8.text:
Perhaps it was because teaching came naturally to Mr Stelling, that he set
about it with that uniformity of method and independence of circumstances which
distinguish the actions of animals understood to be under the immediate
teaching of nature. Mr Broderip’s amiable beaver, as that charming
naturalist tells us, busied himself as earnestly in constructing a dam, in a
room up three pair of stairs in London, as if he had been laying his foundation
in a stream or lake in Upper Canada. It was “Binny’s”
function to build; the absence of water or of possible progeny was an accident
for which he was not accountable. With the same unerring instinct Mr Stelling
set to work at his natural method of instilling the Eton Grammar and Euclid
into the mind of Tom Tulliver. This, he considered, was the only basis of solid
instruction; all other means of education were mere charlatanism, and could
produce nothing better than smatterers. Fixed on this firm basis, a man might
observe the display of various or special knowledge made by irregularly
educated people with a pitying smile; all that sort of thing was very well, but
it was impossible these people could form sound opinions. In holding this
conviction Mr Stelling was not biassed, as some tutors have been, by the
excessive accuracy or extent of his own scholarship; and as to his views about
Euclid, no opinion could have been freer from personal partiality. Mr Stelling
was very far from being led astray by enthusiasm, either religious or
intellectual; on the other hand, he had no secret belief that everything was
humbug. He thought religion was a very excellent thing, and Aristotle a great
authority, and deaneries and prebends useful institutions, and Great Britain
the providential bulwark of Protestantism, and faith in the unseen a great
support to afflicted minds; he believed in all these things, as a Swiss
hotel-keeper believes in the beauty of the scenery around him, and in the
pleasure it gives to artistic visitors. And in the same way Mr Stelling
believed in his method of education; he had no doubt that he was doing the very
best thing for Mr Tulliver’s boy. Of course, when the miller talked of
“mapping” and “summing” in a vague and diffident
manner, Mr Stelling had set his mind at rest by an assurance that he understood
what was wanted; for how was it possible the good man could form any reasonable
judgment about the matter? Mr Stelling’s duty was to teach the lad in the
only right way,—indeed he knew no other; he had not wasted his time in
the acquirement of anything abnormal.
c14:p8.summary: Eliot compares Stelling's mechanical teaching method to a beaver building a dam regardless of circumstance, criticizing his inflexible adherence to classical education.
c14:p8.best_quote: Mr Stelling set to work at his natural method of instilling the Eton Grammar and Euclid into the mind of Tom Tulliver

c14:p9.text:
He very soon set down poor Tom as a thoroughly stupid lad; for though by hard
labour he could get particular declensions into his brain, anything so abstract
as the relation between cases and terminations could by no means get such a
lodgment there as to enable him to recognise a chance genitive or dative. This
struck Mr Stelling as something more than natural stupidity; he suspected
obstinacy, or at any rate indifference, and lectured Tom severely on his want
of thorough application. “You feel no interest in what you’re
doing, sir,” Mr Stelling would say, and the reproach was painfully true.
Tom had never found any difficulty in discerning a pointer from a setter, when
once he had been told the distinction, and his perceptive powers were not at
all deficient. I fancy they were quite as strong as those of the Rev. Mr
Stelling; for Tom could predict with accuracy what number of horses were
cantering behind him, he could throw a stone right into the centre of a given
ripple, he could guess to a fraction how many lengths of his stick it would
take to reach across the playground, and could draw almost perfect squares on
his slate without any measurement. But Mr Stelling took no note of these
things; he only observed that Tom’s faculties failed him before the
abstractions hideously symbolised to him in the pages of the Eton Grammar, and
that he was in a state bordering on idiocy with regard to the demonstration
that two given triangles must be equal, though he could discern with great
promptitude and certainty the fact that they  were  equal. Whence Mr
Stelling concluded that Tom’s brain, being peculiarly impervious to
etymology and demonstrations, was peculiarly in need of being ploughed and
harrowed by these patent implements; it was his favourite metaphor, that the
classics and geometry constituted that culture of the mind which prepared it
for the reception of any subsequent crop. I say nothing against Mr
Stelling’s theory; if we are to have one regimen for all minds, his seems
to me as good as any other. I only know it turned out as uncomfortably for Tom
Tulliver as if he had been plied with cheese in order to remedy a gastric
weakness which prevented him from digesting it. It is astonishing what a
different result one gets by changing the metaphor! Once call the brain an
intellectual stomach, and one’s ingenious conception of the classics and
geometry as ploughs and harrows seems to settle nothing. But then it is open to
some one else to follow great authorities, and call the mind a sheet of white
paper or a mirror, in which case one’s knowledge of the digestive process
becomes quite irrelevant. It was doubtless an ingenious idea to call the camel
the ship of the desert, but it would hardly lead one far in training that
useful beast. O Aristotle! if you had had the advantage of being “the
freshest modern” instead of the greatest ancient, would you not have
mingled your praise of metaphorical speech, as a sign of high intelligence,
with a lamentation that intelligence so rarely shows itself in speech without
metaphor,—that we can so seldom declare what a thing is, except by saying
it is something else?
c14:p9.summary: Stelling mistakes Tom's inability to grasp abstract grammar for stupidity, when Tom's perceptual and practical skills are actually exceptional; the narrator critiques the limitations of metaphorical thinking.
c14:p9.best_quote: O Aristotle! if you had had the advantage of being 'the freshest modern' instead of the greatest ancient, would you not have mingled your praise of metaphorical speech, as a sign of high intelligence, with a lamentation that intelligence so rarely shows itself in speech without metaphor

c16:p7.text:
Tom began to look oftener and longer at Philip’s face, for he could see
it without noticing the hump, and it was really not a disagreeable
face,—very old-looking, Tom thought. He wondered how much older Philip
was than himself. An anatomist—even a mere physiognomist—would have
seen that the deformity of Philip’s spine was not a congenital hump, but
the result of an accident in infancy; but you do not expect from Tom any
acquaintance with such distinctions; to him, Philip was simply a humpback. He
had a vague notion that the deformity of Wakem’s son had some relation to
the lawyer’s rascality, of which he had so often heard his father talk
with hot emphasis; and he felt, too, a half-admitted fear of him as probably a
spiteful fellow, who, not being able to fight you, had cunning ways of doing
you a mischief by the sly. There was a humpbacked tailor in the neighbourhood
of Mr Jacobs’s academy, who was considered a very unamiable character,
and was much hooted after by public-spirited boys solely on the ground of his
unsatisfactory moral qualities; so that Tom was not without a basis of fact to
go upon. Still, no face could be more unlike that ugly tailor’s than this
melancholy boy’s face,—the brown hair round it waved and curled at
the ends like a girl’s: Tom thought that truly pitiable. This Wakem was a
pale, puny fellow, and it was quite clear he would not be able to play at
anything worth speaking of; but he handled his pencil in an enviable manner,
and was apparently making one thing after another without any trouble. What was
he drawing? Tom was quite warm now, and wanted something new to be going
forward. It was certainly more agreeable to have an ill-natured humpback as a
companion than to stand looking out of the study window at the rain, and
kicking his foot against the washboard in solitude; something would happen
every day,—“a quarrel or something”; and Tom thought he
should rather like to show Philip that he had better not try his spiteful
tricks on  him . He suddenly walked across the hearth and looked over
Philip’s paper.
c16:p7.summary: Tom begins to observe Philip's actual face and manner, finding him less disagreeable than expected, though Tom's prejudices about deformity and the Wakem name persist, reinforced by memory of a disagreeable humpbacked tailor.
c16:p7.best_quote: There was a humpbacked tailor in the neighbourhood of Mr Jacobs's academy, who was considered a very unamiable character, and was much hooted after by public-spirited boys solely on the ground of his unsatisfactory moral qualities.

c16:p36.text:
“Oh, I don’t mind,” said Philip, unable to choke a laugh;
“I can remember things easily. And there are some lessons I’m very
fond of. I’m very fond of Greek history, and everything about the Greeks.
I should like to have been a Greek and fought the Persians, and then have come
home and have written tragedies, or else have been listened to by everybody for
my wisdom, like Socrates, and have died a grand death.” (Philip, you
perceive, was not without a wish to impress the well-made barbarian with a
sense of his mental superiority.)
c16:p36.summary: Philip expresses his romantic wish to have been an ancient Greek hero and sage, revealing intellectual idealism and a desire to show Tom his mental superiority.
c16:p36.best_quote: I should like to have been a Greek and fought the Persians, and then have come home and have written tragedies, or else have been listened to by everybody for my wisdom, like Socrates, and have died a grand death.

c28:p29.text: “Ay, my little wench, but I shall never live twice o’er.”
c28:p29.summary: Mr Tulliver tells Maggie that even though she loves him, he will never have another chance at life or redemption.
c28:p29.best_quote: Ay, my little wench, but I shall never live twice o'er

c1:p4.text:
Ah, my arms are really benumbed. I have been pressing my elbows on the arms of
my chair, and dreaming that I was standing on the bridge in front of Dorlcote
Mill, as it looked one February afternoon many years ago. Before I dozed off, I
was going to tell you what Mr and Mrs Tulliver were talking about, as they
sat by the bright fire in the left-hand parlour, on that very afternoon I have
been dreaming of.
c1:p4.summary: The narrator awakens from a reverie and announces intention to recount a conversation between Mr. and Mrs. Tulliver on that same February afternoon, revealing the entire opening as nostalgic memory.
